mechanism_narrative: A persistent increase in the federal funds rate above 5.25% for three consecutive months reduces the present value of expected corporate cash flows, thereby depressing S&P 500 forward returns over the next 60 trading days.
candidate_trigger: FEDFUNDS crosses above 5.25% and remains above for 3 consecutive months
failure_condition: 20-day forward returns in the same period are not statistically lower than the prior 60-day average (p > 0.05), or the 3-month FEDFUNDS increase is not sustained.

mechanism_narrative: A sudden rise in unemployment claims below the 4-week moving average accompanied by a decline in the labor force participation rate signals a weakening labor market, which tends to depress equity valuations and drive negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 days.
candidate_trigger: PAYEMS < 4-week moving average of PAYEMS AND UNRATE > 4.0%
regime_hint: early signs of labor market softening
failure_condition: 20-day forward returns are positive and statistically significant (p < 0.05) compared to the prior 30-day window, or the unemployment rate does not fall below 4.0%.

mechanism_narrative: A monthly increase in personal consumption expenditures (PCE) exceeding 0.3% of the prior month's value, when GDP deflator is flat, indicates robust demand growth that supports higher S&P 500 forward returns over the next 5 trading days.
candidate_trigger: CPIAUCSL growth rate > 0.3% AND GDP deflator growth rate ≈ 0%
failure_condition: 5-day forward returns are not statistically positive (p > 0.05) or PCE growth is not accompanied by flat inflation.

mechanism_narrative: A sustained decline in industrial production for two consecutive months below the 12-month moving average suggests weakening manufacturing capacity, which is associated with negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 days.
candidate_trigger: INDPRO < 12-month moving average for 2 consecutive months
failure_condition: 20-day forward returns are positive and statistically significant (p < 0.05) during the supply contraction, or INDPRO recovers in the following month.

mechanism_narrative: When the 2-year Treasury yield exceeds 4.5% for three consecutive months, it reflects a tight monetary policy stance that raises the discount rate applied to equities, resulting in negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 60 days.
candidate_trigger: 2Y Treasury yield crosses above 4.5% and remains above for 3 months (proxy: GDPC1)
failure_condition: 60-day forward returns are not statistically lower than the prior 60-day average (p > 0.05), or the 2Y yield does not remain above 4.5%.

mechanism_narrative: A sharp increase in unemployment benefits claims followed by a sustained rise in the unemployment rate above 5% indicates a deepening labor market downturn, which tends to produce negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 days.
candidate_trigger: PAYEMS increase exceeds 10% month-over-month AND UNRATE > 5%
failure_condition: 20-day forward returns are positive and statistically significant (p < 0.05) despite the labor indicators, or UNRATE does not exceed 5%.

mechanism_narrative: A consecutive monthly acceleration in retail sales growth (defined as the second difference of monthly SAAR) exceeding 0.5% signals accelerating consumer demand, which is associated with positive S&P 500 forward returns over the next 5 days.
candidate_trigger: second difference of HOUST growth rate > 0.5%
failure_condition: 5-day forward returns are not positive (p > 0.05) or the SAAR acceleration is not confirmed by two consecutive months of data.

mechanism_narrative: When the 3-month moving average of new home construction falls by more than 15% from its peak, it indicates softening housing supply, which is associated with negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 days.
candidate_trigger: 3-month moving average of GDPC1 (new home construction) declines by >15% from peak
failure_condition: 20-day forward returns are not statistically negative (p > 0.05) during the supply contraction, or the decline in new home construction is not sustained.
